newsitem.title: USA: SEC votes to curb abuses of offshore offering rule.
newsitem.headline: SEC votes to curb abuses of offshore offering rule.

text.p: The U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission has voted unanimously to curb problems that have arisen under the agency's six-year-old rule that exempts U.S. corporations from registering offshore offerings.
The SEC adopted a rule on Wednesday that requires firms to report offshore sales of equities by U.S. firms within 15 days of the sale.
And in a bid to discourage security offerings from going offshore in the first place, the SEC also voted to ease reporting requirements for companies making acquisitions.

SEC Chairman Arthur Levitt told a public meeting of the SEC that the new rules would address "problematic practices" that have arisen under Regulation S, the SEC rule that exempts U.S. corporations from registering offshore offerings.
"This is one safe harbour with too many pirates in it. We're determined to sweep it clear," Levitt said. He added that the actions "are not a cure for what ails Reg S."
"The markets are on notice," Levitt said.
"I am committed to addressing these abuses more directly - the Commission will consider additional initiatives in the near future," Levitt said.
Until Wednesday, companies that registered with the SEC were not required to disclose sales of unregistered securities in the current or periodic reports they filed with the commission.
The result has been to "encourage abusive offshore offering practices," SEC staff said.
While requiring offshore securities sales be reported within 15 days of sale on Form 8-K, private placements generally must be reported quarterly, under the new rule.
Firms must report the price and amount of securities sold, sale date, type of purchasers and other specific information, SEC said.

To encourage more domestic offerings, the SEC dropped a previous requirement that companies supply audited financial statements of businesses they acquire or are likely to acquire when the target company has assets totalling more than 10 percent of the total assets of the company seeking to buy.
"This requirement has been cited by both domestic and foreign companies as a barrier to conducting a registered U.S. public offering," SEC staff said.

Wednesday's amendments say firms can proceed with registered offerings without supplying financial statements for the businesses they acquire as long as those businesses were no more than half the size of the corporations buying them.
